phase3_findings.description: The new `await _conversation_baseline(...)` runs inside the per-conversation turn context manager but outside the `try` block at line 408 that owns the function's error taxonomy. Its two awaits, `agent.user_resolver.resolve_user` and `agent.conversation_store.get_conversation`, have no handler, so anything they raise passes `server.py` (which only intercepts `AgentRunError`) and reaches the MCP client as a raw exception string instead of the sanitized `_INTERNAL_ERROR_MESSAGE` the docstring at lines 332-334 promises. Unreachable with the shipped `_StaticUserResolver` and `BoundedConversationStore`, both of which are trivial and cannot raise; an embedder-supplied resolver or store reaches it. The sibling rollback path guards this same seam.

The sentence "the cleanup in the `finally:` above still runs on that same thread, before the exception surfaces at the `await`" holds for an exception raised inside the threaded body but is false for the cancellation case the same paragraph describes. Because `asyncio.to_thread` cannot interrupt a running worker, a `CancelledError` surfaces at the `await` immediately while the thread's `finally` cleanup runs later. Capped behavior-inert by Phase 4.1.5 (first-conjunct held, limb-one held, limb-two held).

The inline comment repeats the same imprecision: "teardown runs on the thread that owns the connection, before any exception surfaces at the await". The thread-affinity half is correct; the "before any exception surfaces at the await" half is false under cancellation. The MySQL and Postgres runners carry no equivalent sentence. Capped behavior-inert by Phase 4.1.5.

The rewritten item attributes `loop.shutdown_default_executor()` to `uvicorn/_compat.py` while the issue's verified premise records that call in `uvicorn/server.py`. One agent could not check it (uvicorn is outside the workspace); prflow:comment-analyzer read the installed `uvicorn/_compat.py` 0.54.0 and reported the claim correct, so this stands only as an unresolved cross-check. Capped behavior-inert by Phase 4.1.5.

The added sentence asserts "so its health check keeps answering". `/healthz` is served only by the HTTP transport's path normalizer, while the preceding paragraph walks the reader through stdio mode, where no health endpoint exists. True for HTTP, vacuous for the adjacent stdio reader; the criterion asks only for the "does not stop the server from accepting other requests" part. Capped by Phase 4.1.5 at important (limb-two not held, docs/external is published), weighed at the lower of that and its original suggestion.

Every `False` return from the rollback logs one INFO line, but `BoundedConversationStore.truncate_messages` returns `False` for three distinct reasons. One of them, a user-id mismatch, means the conversation still exists and still holds the cancelled call's messages, a genuinely failed rollback that the sibling branch treats as ERROR-worthy. The log cannot distinguish the three. Unreachable today because the shipped resolver yields one user id.

`_ConversationQueueEntry` bundles a lock and a public mutable `users` counter but owns no behavior. Its refcount invariant is maintained by two module-level functions, hand-written arithmetic at two call sites, and a separate dict-registration site. `_release_queue_entry` tests `users <= 0`, folding a double release into the same branch as the correct zero case, so a future double-release would delete the entry silently. Behavior on the diff's paths is correct.

`truncate_messages` is declared only on `BoundedConversationStore`, not on the `ConversationStore` base class, so the production caller probes for it at run time and degrades to an ERROR log. Support for synchronous cancel rollback is therefore a runtime requirement rather than a typed one, and a type checker cannot warn an embedder that the framework default store loses the rollback.

`truncate_messages` deletes the tail of `conversation.messages` from outside the model, while `add_message` couples that list to `updated_at` by stamping both together. After a rollback `updated_at` still reflects the cancelled turn whose messages are gone, and that timestamp is the key `list_conversations` sorts on.

`_conversation_turn`'s yielded `str | None` carries two decisions at once (which id to roll back, and whether a lock was taken), and the caller keeps the baseline as two independently initialized locals with an empty string standing for "no baseline". An empty user id is a representable but illegal state kept from `truncate_messages` only by the `queued_id is not None` guard, where it would match no conversation and return `False` as a silently skipped rollback.

The comment above `_LIVENESS_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` and `_assert_loop_live_while`'s docstring both claim a pre-fix run fails by the `asyncio.wait_for` probe timing out, which cannot happen: `wait_for`'s timer runs on the same loop the blocking call would hold. On a pre-change tree the test instead fails on `assert not blocked.done()` after the fake driver's own thirty-second wait. The tests work; the stated reason is wrong and will mislead anyone tuning that timeout. Capped behavior-inert by Phase 4.1.5.

`test_profile_row_cap_reaches_offloaded_runner` pins the per-request profile row cap for `PostgresRunner` only. MySQL and SQLite gained the same `asyncio.to_thread` hop and each read `effective_row_cap` inside the thread, so switching either to `loop.run_in_executor` (the mistake all three in-code comments warn against) would silently fetch the base `max_rows` with no failing test. The liveness tests for those runners pass regardless of the cap.

The `stream_request` docstring still says it "Yields text chunks as they arrive", while the new implementation drains the whole stream on a worker thread and yields the collected text afterwards. The inline comment below it describes the new behavior correctly. Raised by the code-reviewer as a sub-threshold note. Capped behavior-inert by Phase 4.1.5.

## Verdict: APPROVE with notes (one Important note and twelve suggestions, all below the configured threshold)

This PR is ready to merge: every one of the eleven acceptance criteria verified as met, no checklist item failed, and the only substantive note is an error-handling narrowing that the shipped components cannot reach today.

Rule applied: rule 6 — a finding or checklist FAIL below the threshold, an exempt finding, or an INCONCLUSIVE item → APPROVE with notes

## Code Review Findings

### 🟠 Important / Major

1. In `src/sqllens/tools/query_database.py`, the new `await _conversation_baseline(...)` at lines 400-406 runs inside the per-conversation turn context manager but outside the `try` block at line 408 that owns this function's error taxonomy. The two awaits it performs, `agent.user_resolver.resolve_user` and `agent.conversation_store.get_conversation`, therefore have no handler: anything they raise travels past `server.py`, which only intercepts `AgentRunError`, and reaches the MCP client as a raw exception string instead of the sanitized `_INTERNAL_ERROR_MESSAGE` the same function's docstring promises. With the shipped `_StaticUserResolver` and `BoundedConversationStore` both calls are trivial and cannot raise, so behavior is correct today; an embedder supplying its own resolver or store would reach it, and the sibling rollback path guards exactly this seam while the baseline path does not. (raised by 2/6 agents)

### 🟡 Suggestion / Minor (12)

Because `asyncio.to_thread` cannot interrupt a running worker, a `CancelledError` surfaces at the `await` immediately while the thread's `finally` cleanup runs later, possibly minutes later. A reader asking whether the connection is closed by the time a cancelled request returns is led to the wrong answer. acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] While a `query_database` call is blocked inside a synchronous Anthropic client call or inside a synchronous database driver call (connect, execute or fetch), the event loop keeps running other tasks, and the HTTP transport answers `GET /healthz`. This holds for non-streaming and streaming Anthropic requests and for each of the Postgres, MySQL and SQLite runners.
- [ ] Two `query_database` calls with different conversation ids, each blocked inside a synchronous Anthropic or database call, are blocked at the same time: neither waits for the other call to finish before entering its own blocking call.
- [ ] Two `query_database` calls with the same conversation id do not overlap: the second call's agent run starts only after the first call has returned, failed or been cancelled. When both calls return or fail, the conversation's history afterwards holds the first call's messages followed by the second call's messages.
- [ ] After every call on a conversation has returned, failed or been cancelled — including a call cancelled while it was waiting for its turn — the server holds no per-conversation queue entry for that conversation id.
- [ ] When a `query_database` call is cancelled while it is running, the conversation holds none of the messages that call added and keeps every message that was in it when the cancelled call's turn began (after any earlier call on that conversation id finished). The next call on that conversation id runs with that history.
- [ ] When a `query_database` call is cancelled, the tool function raises the cancellation and returns no result.
- [ ] For the same conversation id, the same sequence of Anthropic responses and the same query results, a `query_database` call returns the same text content and the same `_meta` as before this change, apart from the duration values in the agent trace. This holds for both streaming and non-streaming Anthropic requests.
- [ ] An Anthropic API error raised during a call still produces an `isError: true` result, and a database error or statement timeout raised by a runner still produces a failed `run_sql` step that the agent can re-plan from, as before this change.
- [ ] A database query run under a profile whose `max_rows` is lower than the base config's fetches at most that profile's `max_rows` plus one rows from the driver.
- [ ] The change leaves these as they are: - It adds no interruption of work already running on a worker thread. A cancelled call's database query keeps running until it finishes or the engine's statement timeout stops it. Nothing but the query's own end stops it when `statement_timeout_ms = 0`, or when it is a MySQL statement other than `SELECT`, which MySQL's `MAX_EXECUTION_TIME` does not cover. A cancelled call's Anthropic request keeps running, and is billed, until it returns. Server shutdown waits for such threads. - It adds no thread pool of its own. Anthropic calls and database queries share asyncio's default executor, so beyond its thread count further calls wait for a free thread. The ChromaDB memory store keeps its own two-thread pool. - It leaves the synchronous memory-store calls of `import_memory` and the memory-administration MCP tools on the event loop, so those tools still block it while they run. - It leaves the scratch CSV write after each query, `df.to_csv`, and the read-only and row-level-security guards' SQL parsing on the event loop. - It adds no progress notifications and no acknowledge-now / fetch-later job API. A `query_database` call still holds its request open until the agent run ends, so a question that takes longer than a client's timeout still times out for that client.
- [ ] After the change: - `docs/internal/mcp-server/tools.md` states that `query_database`'s Anthropic calls and database queries run on worker threads, that calls sharing a conversation id run one at a time, that a cancelled call's messages are removed from its conversation, and that `import_memory` and the memory-administration tools still block the event loop. - `docs/internal/database-connectors/cleanup-error-handling.md` and `docs/internal/database-connectors/read-only-safety.md` state that a cancelled request's database query keeps running on its worker thread until it finishes or the engine's statement timeout stops it. - `docs/external/getting-started.md` states that a question waiting on the AI service or the database does not stop the server from accepting other requests, and that `import_memory` and the memory-administration tools can still briefly block them.

checklist.claim: Server shutdown waits for in-flight worker threads via `loop.shutdown_default_executor()`, waiting indefinitely on Python 3.11 and up to five minutes on 3.12+, because uvicorn runs the server through `asyncio.run` / `asyncio.Runner` (`uvicorn/_compat.py`).
checklist.source_excerpt: uvicorn runs the server through `asyncio.run` / `asyncio.Runner` (`uvicorn/_compat.py`), which calls `loop.shutdown_default_executor()` on the way out. How long it waits depends on the interpreter — on Python 3.11 that call takes no timeout and waits indefinitely; on 3.12+ `asyncio.run` passes it a five-minute cap.
